Monday, 4 April 2033. Ioana is looking for a coordinator for the collaboration between her firm and Arhimar in Bucharest. She meets Sorina Matei, a young Romanian architect living in Lyon.
Good morning, Ms Matei. Have a seat. Can you tell me about your background?
Of course. Having studied architecture in Cluj, I came to Lyon four years ago. I learnt the trade by working in a small firm in Croix-Rousse.
And why did you apply to us?
I read the article about the Stan house. The project was introduced to me by a friend, and I knew straight away that I wanted to take part.
What, in your opinion, are your main qualities? And your weaknesses?
I’m organised and versatile. As for my weaknesses… I’m sometimes too demanding of myself. But I’m learning to delegate.
The job involves frequent travel to Bucharest. Is that a problem?
Not at all. While living in Lyon, I keep very strong ties with Romania. My mother lives in Bucharest.
Very good. The position is offered on a permanent contract, with a three-month probation period. What are your salary expectations?
I was thinking of thirty-eight thousand euros gross a year. And if possible, one day of remote work a week.
(she smiles) Remote work has already been granted to one of our architects on Fridays. I don’t see why you would be refused it.
Thank you. And what would the start date be?
2 May, if you’re available. I’ll send you the contract this week. Welcome to Fabre & Popescu.

In France, salary is usually discussed GROSS per year (“trente-huit mille euros brut par an”), not net per month as in Romania.
A polite way to ask for something: “Si c’était possible, j’aimerais…” or “Serait-il envisageable de… ?” (Would it be possible to…?).

Amina had lied on the Grenoble train. The adult beginners’ orchestra didn’t exist. But a week later, it did. She had found a hall, a time, a conductor and a budget. The hall was the Salle Hélène Morel, free on Thursday evenings. The time was seven to nine p.m. The conductor was Théo, who had said yes before she finished her sentence. And the budget was zero euros.

Zero euros was possible thanks to Gérard Thiébaut. The old luthier had heard the news from Julien and had sent from Mirecourt, within a week, eleven repaired instruments he had been keeping in his workshop “for a good occasion”. Two violins, a viola, a cello, a flute, two clarinets, a dented trumpet, a trombone and two drums. In the crate there was a note: “For the big children.”

That left finding the musicians. Amina did no advertising. She simply pinned a sheet on the noticeboard of the Salle Hélène Morel: “Thursday orchestra. Adult beginners. No level required. Free.” Underneath there were fourteen empty lines for sign-ups. She had made a spreadsheet, of course. But for once she had wanted to start with a sheet of paper and a pen.

The first sign-up came the same day. It was Inès’s mother. Her name was Nadia. She was forty-four, had worked nights at the hospital for twenty years, and had never touched an instrument in her life. She had written her name in very careful capital letters, and beside it, in the “instrument wanted” column, she had written: “The flute. Like Sami.”

Inès found out that same evening, seeing her mother come home with a smile she had never seen on her. She said nothing. She went to her room, took her old flute tutor book, the one she had used for three months before choosing the clarinet, and put it on the kitchen table. On the cover she stuck a little note: “For Mum. Start at page 4. Pages 1 to 3 are boring.”

The next day, Isabelle signed up for the cello. She was fifty-nine. She explained to Amina that her mother had always regretted not learning the cello, and that she herself had spent her life listening to others play. “I’m at the age when you stop putting things off,” she said. Amina wrote the sentence in the “comments” column. She thought it sounded good.

The third sign-up surprised everyone. Bernard Delorme, the former opponent of the hall, seventy years old, turned up one Tuesday morning at the Croix-Rousse office with an old photo in his hand. It showed a twelve-year-old boy in uniform, with a trumpet, in the Vénissieux municipal brass band, in 1975. “That’s me,” he said. “I stopped at fourteen. I’d like to know whether I still have the breath.”

His wife, Monique, had thought it was a joke. Bernard Delorme, the man who had voted against the hall, was going to play the trumpet in that very hall? She laughed for ten minutes. Then she went up to the attic without a word and came down with an old cardboard box. Inside was the 1975 band uniform, carefully folded, with its gold buttons. She had kept it for forty years without telling him.

Then the names followed one another. A baker from La Duchère who wanted to play the drum. A retired bus driver who had dreamt of the clarinet ever since he heard Inès at the Odéon. The school caretaker, the one Inès’s mother had hugged on exam-results day, who chose the trombone “because it’s the biggest”. A young father, two students, a pharmacist. In ten days, the fourteen lines were full.

The last line had been filled in with a fine grey handwriting that Amina recognised at once: “Bertrand Vidal. Violin. Level: to be reviewed.” Below, in the “comments” column, he had added: “Arriving on the 17:04 train. Leaving on the 21:34.” Amina looked at the sheet for a long time. Then she copied the line into her spreadsheet without changing a comma.

The first rehearsal took place on Thursday 3 March 2033. It was raining. The fourteen beginners arrived one by one, intimidated, shaking their umbrellas, looking at the big empty hall the way you look at a swimming pool before diving in. Théo was waiting for them in the middle, under the skylight, with an enormous smile. He had set out fourteen chairs in a semicircle. On each chair there was an instrument and a label with a first name.

In the front row of the audience seats there were two spectators. Mrs Roux, eighty-seven, in her wheelchair, who had come with an old wooden metronome that had belonged to her husband Lucien. And Rose-Hélène, who would turn five the next day and who had obtained special permission from her parents to stay up until nine. Théo had appointed her “conductor’s assistant”. She took her role very seriously.

Théo made no speech. He asked everyone to pick up their instrument and play a single note, any note, all at the same time, when he raised his hand. He raised his hand. The noise that filled the Salle Hélène Morel that evening was indescribable. A mixture of a wounded duck, a creaking door, a lorry horn and a cat someone had trodden on. Rose-Hélène covered her ears.

There was a dismayed silence. Then the baker burst out laughing. Then the bus driver. Then everyone. Bernard Delorme laughed so hard he had to sit down, his trumpet on his knees. Even Mr Vidal was smiling, his violin under his chin. Théo waited for the laughter to die down. Then he said: “Perfect. That’s the sound of our first day. In two months, we’ll play the waltz.”

Nobody believed him. But Théo had a method, the same one he had used with the La Duchère children six years earlier. He never started with theory. He started with listening. During the first hour, the beginners hardly played at all. They listened. Théo had them close their eyes and recognise the others’ instruments. Then he taught them one note, just one, and they played it together until it sounded right.

Coming out of the first rehearsal, in the rain, the fourteen beginners didn’t want to leave. They stayed on the pavement outside the hall, still laughing about the noise they had made. The pharmacist suggested setting up a group chat on their phones. The bus driver suggested the name. By that evening the group was called “The Thursday Ducks”. By midnight it already had two hundred messages.

Théo had given them just one piece of homework for the following week: listen to music for ten minutes a day, eyes closed, doing nothing else. Not while driving, not while cooking, not while reading. Just listening. Half the group found it the hardest homework of their lives. The school caretaker admitted he had fallen asleep three times. Théo said it was a good start.

Mr Vidal was by far the best. Week after week, his fingers rediscovered what they had learnt forty years earlier. But he never pushed himself forward. He sat in the back row and discreetly helped the two student violinists place their fingers. He always arrived on the 17:04 train and always left on the 21:34. He never missed a single rehearsal.

On the 17:04 train, a passenger once asked him what he was carrying in that black case. Mr Vidal hesitated. For twenty-two years, when people asked what he did, he had answered: “Magistrate at the Court of Audit.” That day he answered: “I’m going to my rehearsal.” The passenger smiled. He spent the rest of the journey looking out of the window, surprised to hear himself say that sentence.

After each rehearsal he had twenty minutes before his train. Amina, who lived near the station, had got into the habit of walking there with him. They had a coffee at the counter of the station buffet at ten past nine, always the same one, standing up. They spoke little. About the rehearsal, figures, the weather. Then he got on his train and Amina walked home. It had become a habit. They had never decided it.

Amina herself didn’t play. She came to every rehearsal, sat next to Mrs Roux with her computer on her knees, and kept the spreadsheet of attendance, progress and instruments up to date. Théo had suggested ten times that she take up an instrument. She had refused ten times. She said an orchestra needed someone who counted. Théo replied that that was precisely the conductor’s job.

Bernard Delorme had got his breath back faster than expected. After three weeks he could play a whole scale without stopping. After five he played so loudly that Théo had to ask him to move to the back of the hall, behind the trombone. He didn’t take offence. He said he had spent forty years making noise on the town council, and was pleased to be making useful noise at last.

One evening, Bernard Delorme called Mrs Faure in Grenoble to tell her the news. The two former opponents of the music halls had met at the opening in January and wrote to each other from time to time. Mrs Faure didn’t believe a word of his story. He had to send her a video of himself playing a scale. She replied with a single message: “I’m signing up in Grenoble. Saxophone. Don’t tell anyone.”

Nadia, Inès’s mother, was the one who progressed most slowly. She worked nights, slept during the day, and had no time to practise. She arrived on Thursdays with dark circles under her eyes, and often couldn’t get a single sound out of her flute. One evening, after a month, she wanted to give up. She put the flute back in its case and told Théo she wasn’t made for this.

That evening, someone else had come to the rehearsal. Sami, fourteen now, the little flautist who hardly ever spoke. Inès had told him her mother wanted to learn “like him”. He went up to Nadia without a word. He took out his own flute. He showed her, very slowly, how to place her lips, how to blow, not hard, just a thread of air. Then he said his longest sentence of the year: “Let’s try together.”

They tried together. For half an hour, in a corner of the hall, a fourteen-year-old boy and a forty-four-year-old woman blew into two flutes side by side. After twenty-five minutes, a sound came out of Nadia’s flute. A weak, trembling sound, but a real one. A G. Nadia burst into tears. Sami nodded, satisfied, then left without saying goodbye. Nadia never talked about giving up again.

Isabelle had chosen the cello for a reason she told only Julien. Sorting through her mother’s things, she had found in the 1971 logbook a sentence written by Henri the day after they met: “She has a cellist’s hands.” Odile had never played. Isabelle had decided that someone in the family had to find out whether Henri was right.

Isabelle practised in the evenings in her mother’s flat, sitting in Odile’s armchair, the cello between her knees. On the other side of the landing, Rose-Hélène could hear her. After a week, she got into the habit of crossing over with her key on its blue ribbon, sitting on the floor in front of Isabelle and telling her, very seriously, when a note was out of tune. She was right every time. Isabelle ended up calling her “my teacher”.

The school caretaker practised the trombone in the evenings in the empty school courtyard, after closing time. The first week, the neighbours called the police twice. The second week, they opened their windows to shout. The third week, someone applauded. The fourth, an old lady on the third floor brought him down hot tea in a thermos. She asked him whether he knew any Édith Piaf songs.

Meanwhile, life went on. On 4 April, Ioana had interviewed Sorina Matei and hired her the same day. Sorina was organised, versatile, and played the piano. On the first Thursday after she started, Ioana took her to the Salle Hélène Morel. There was no piano in the Thursday orchestra. The next day there was one: Amina had found an old upright piano at a school that was closing down.

On Sorina’s first Thursday, Théo asked her to play something so the others could hear the piano. She sat down without music and played a very simple Romanian folk tune her grandmother used to sing to her when she was little. In the middle of the melody, the baker started tapping the rhythm on her drum. Then the bus driver found two notes on the clarinet. That was how the Romanian tune got into the programme.

On Saturday 16 April, the whole family set off for Brest. The second of the network’s eight new halls was opening its doors, in the old fish market in the harbour. Yves Le Goff, eighty-nine, had been invited to cut the ribbon. He had refused three times, saying he was just an old sailor. Then he had accepted, on condition that he be called “sailor” and not “sir”.

The hall was called “La Criée”, in memory of the fish auctions held there for a century. Radu had kept the big iron beams, the white wall tiles and the ceiling hooks where nets used to be hung. Through the big skylight you could see the gulls circling in the grey sky. It still smelled a little of the sea. Yves said it was the most beautiful concert hall in the world.

The Brest children’s orchestra played Henri’s waltz, accompanied for the occasion by a bagad: a Breton band of bagpipes, bombardes and drums. The result was so powerful that the windows shook. At the third verse, the bagpipes fell silent along with the children. Eight bars of silence. And in that silence, in the harbour, a foghorn sounded. A real ship. Nobody had planned it.

Yves Le Goff closed his eyes. He said quietly that it was Henri saying hello. Nobody dared contradict him. Rose-Hélène whistled after the foghorn, and the bagad started up again with even more gusto. After the concert, Yves made galettes for three hundred people in a crêperie in the harbour, whose owner was the son of one of his old shipmates. It was two in the morning when he finally put down his pan.

The next morning, Isabelle and Yves Le Goff walked along the quay in the cold wind. Yves walked slowly, leaning on his cane. He showed her the dock where Henri’s ship used to berth in the seventies. Isabelle told him she was learning the cello. Yves stopped. He said Henri would have been pleased. Then he added that Henri always said Odile had a cellist’s hands. Isabelle didn’t answer. She already knew.

Back in Lyon, the Thursday orchestra had made spectacular progress. Théo had set a date for a first concert: Saturday 7 May, at the Salle Hélène Morel, in front of the families. On the programme, three pieces. A very simple march, a Romanian folk tune that Sorina had arranged for the occasion, and, of course, Henri’s waltz. With the silence. The fourteen beginners were terrified.

In the meantime, there was a birthday. On 4 May, little Yves turned one. It was also Radu and Lucia’s third wedding anniversary. The whole family gathered at their place for afternoon tea. Little Yves put both hands in his cake, tasted the cream, pulled a face, then ate the lot. His godfather, who had come from Nantes, gave him a little striped sailor top, size one year. It was already too small.

That day, little Yves also took his first steps, exactly like his cousin Henri-Ion two years earlier, on his birthday. He stood up holding on to his godfather’s leg, let go of the trousers, and walked three steps to Rose-Hélène, who was holding her harmonica out in front of her like bait. Yves Le Goff declared it was a sailor’s gait. Nobody knew what that meant.

On Saturday 7 May, at four p.m., the Salle Hélène Morel was full. But that day the audience was not the usual audience. In the front row were the sixty children of the La Duchère orchestra, who had come to listen to their parents, grandparents, neighbours, their baker and their school caretaker. For once, they were the ones sitting down. They had brought signs. One said: “Go, Mum!”

It was Inès holding it. She was sitting in the middle of the front row, her clarinet on her knees, looking at her mother with a mixture of pride and panic. Nadia, on stage, was holding her flute with both hands like a lifebuoy. Next to Inès, Sami wasn’t looking at anyone. But when Nadia caught his eye, he gave her a thumbs-up. Just once, very quickly. Nadia breathed.

Backstage, a quarter of an hour before the concert, nobody spoke. The baker was gripping her sticks. The bus driver was wiping his clarinet for the tenth time. Bernard Delorme had put his 1975 band uniform back on, a little tight around the stomach. Théo gathered them in a circle. He gave them a single piece of advice: “If you get lost, don’t panic. Stop playing and listen to the others. The silence will bring you back.”

Théo stepped onto the platform. He greeted the audience. He turned to his fourteen musicians, plus Sorina at the piano. He raised his baton. And the Thursday orchestra played its march. It wasn’t perfect. The trombone came in too early. The baker’s drum lost the rhythm twice. But it was recognisable, it moved forward, and at the end the sixty children stood up yelling as if in a stadium.

Then came the Romanian tune. Sorina had chosen it with Grandma in mind, who used to sing it while peeling vegetables. Ioana recognised it from the first notes. She took her phone and video-called Iași, without a word, turning the screen towards the stage. Two thousand kilometres away, in her kitchen, Grandma put down her knife. And she began to sing along with the orchestra, quietly, the words she had known since childhood.

When the tune ended, Grandma asked Ioana, through the screen, to send her the score. She wanted to take it to Bucharest, to Viorica, whose friend she had become, so that the first piece played on the restored piano would be that tune. Sorina, who had heard, promised to write it out neatly by hand before the evening. She did. Grandma had it framed in Iași.

Finally, Théo announced Henri’s waltz. A respectful silence fell over the hall. Everyone at La Duchère knew the waltz. Everyone knew the silence. The children of the orchestra had played it hundreds of times. But they had never heard it played by their parents. Rose-Hélène, sitting on a chair next to Théo, harmonica in hand, was waiting for her moment, very focused.

They played. Slowly, much more slowly than the children. Mr Vidal, in the back row, carried the other violins without them noticing. Isabelle held her bass line on the cello, frowning, counting the beats under her breath. Bernard Delorme played so softly, for once, that you could hardly hear him. And Nadia, in the middle, held her flute part, note after note, without missing a single one.

At the third verse, at the moment of silence, the fourteen beginners stopped. Not quite together: the trombone went on half a second too long. But they stopped. Eight bars. Rose-Hélène raised her harmonica. She was going to play the three notes, as always. But before she could blow, a sound crossed the hall. A clear, crisp, tiny sound, from the front row of the audience seats. Ting.

Everyone turned round. Sitting next to Mrs Roux, her computer closed on her knees, Amina was holding a small metal triangle in her left hand and a beater in her right. Nobody had seen her pick it up. Nobody knew she had it. She had just struck a single note. Just one. Exactly on the first beat of the fifth bar. In the middle of the silence. Like a full stop in the middle of a sentence.

Théo looked at her, astonished. Amina held his gaze, very calm, her cheeks a little pink. Later she would explain that she had calculated the exact moment over two months, listening to every rehearsal, and that according to her calculations the silence lacked a marker in the middle so that the beginners wouldn’t get lost counting. It was a question of efficiency, she would say. Nobody would believe her.

Rose-Hélène didn’t hesitate. Four bars later, at the end of the silence, she played her three notes, as always. Then she whistled the next three. And the Thursday orchestra set off again, together this time, with nobody getting lost. Amina’s marker had worked. In the back row, Mr Vidal smiled as he played. He had understood before anyone else to whom the triangle was dedicated.

At the end of the waltz, the sixty children stood up. Not yelling this time. In silence. They applauded for a long time, standing, without a shout, the way you applaud at the end of a very great concert. Nadia was crying on stage, her flute against her chest. Bernard Delorme was bowing like a general. Isabelle was gripping her bow so tightly her fingers were white. And the baker was laughing and laughing, unable to stop.

After the concert there was a snack in the hall. The children all wanted to try their parents’ instruments. The parents all wanted advice from their children. Yanis was explaining to Isabelle how to hold her bow. Inès was showing her mother how to breathe before a long phrase. And Sami, sitting in a corner with Nadia, was playing her something very gentle that nobody else could hear.

Mr Vidal came over to Amina with two paper cups of coffee. Black, no sugar, for her. Two sugars, for him. He asked her how long she had had that triangle. She replied that Gérard Thiébaut had slipped it into the crate of instruments in March, with a note addressed to her. She hadn’t told anyone. She had kept it in her bag for two months. He asked what the note said. She didn’t answer.

But that evening, as she was packing her bag, Julien saw a small folded piece of paper fall out, which Amina picked up very quickly. He had time to read three words, written in the old luthier’s shaky hand: “Even the accountants.” Julien said nothing. He thought of Yves, who said accountants were like sailors, that they all had a song hidden away somewhere. Amina’s fitted into a single note. It was perfect.

That night, Nadia left for the hospital for her shift, as every Saturday. In her bag, next to her uniform, was her flute. Around three in the morning, during her break, an old patient who couldn’t sleep called her. She was frightened. Nadia sat down beside her bed. She took out the flute and played, very softly, the only note she could play perfectly. A G. The old lady fell asleep.

That evening, on the way back to rue d’Austerlitz, Rose-Hélène asked her father whether she was still the conductor’s assistant, now that Amina played in the silence too. Julien said yes, of course. The silence was big enough for two. Rose-Hélène thought about it. Then she said it was true: there were eight bars. Four for Amina, four for her. She thought that was a fair share.

The following Thursday, at seven p.m., the Thursday orchestra resumed its rehearsals. There was a fifteenth chair in the semicircle, next to Mr Vidal’s. On the chair there was a little metal triangle and a label with a first name, in Théo’s handwriting: “Amina”. Amina looked at it for a long time from the doorway. Then she put her computer down on an audience chair and went to sit in her place.
